title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 116 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 579–581 (Night 116, continuing directly from nights-115), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 116 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. Alone in the empty pavilion, he waits three hours for the woman from the window; she does not come. Starved after days of lovesickness, he eats from the dishes laid out there — roast chickens, sweetmeat, pomegranate seeds, baklava, qaṭāʾif — and falls asleep. He wakes in the full sun on the bare marble, with salt and charcoal laid on his belly. At home his cousin ʿAzīza, weeping over verses of her own love for him, reads the signs: the salt says he is insipid, a lover who sleeps; the charcoal says, God blacken your face, you are a child who cares only for eating and sleeping. He begs her to tell him what to do, for she loves him dearly. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixteenth after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixteenth night,
sentences.n: al-sādisata ʿashara, “sixteenth”: as in the nights before, the print has the masculine عشر beside the feminine night, and it is vocalised as printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الشَّابَّ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَهِمْتُ بِذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَفَرِحْتُ غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ لَكِنِّي مَا وَجَدْتُ فِيهِ أَحَدًا مِنْ خَلْقِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَلَمْ أَرَ عَبْدًا وَلَا جَارِيَةً وَلَا مَنْ يُعَانِي هَذِة الْأُمُورَ وَلَا مَنْ يَحْرُسُ تِلْكَ الْحَوَائِجَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-himtu bi-dhālika al-makāni wa-fariḥtu ghāyata al-faraḥi lākinnī mā wajadtu fīhi aḥadan min khalqi allāhi taʿālā wa-lam ara ʿabdan wa-lā jāriyatan wa-lā man yuʿānī hādhihi al-umūra wa-lā man yaḥrusu tilka al-ḥawāʾija
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth said to Tāj al-Mulūk: And I was enraptured with that place and rejoiced the utmost of rejoicing; but I did not find in it anyone of the creatures of God, exalted is He, and I did not see a slave nor a slave-girl, nor anyone who tends these matters, nor anyone who guards those things.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man said to Tāj al-Mulūk: I was enchanted by the place and overjoyed. But I found no one there, not one of God’s creatures: no slave, no slave-girl, no one to see to all these things and no one to guard them.
sentences.n: fa-himtu, “and I was enraptured”: the print marks the word فهِمتُ so that it is not read fahimtu, “I understood”; it is hāma, “to be lost in love or wonder”, and it takes bi- for what one is lost in. The night opens by going back over the last lines of the night before. al-ḥawāʾij: “needs, things needed”, here the furnishings and provisions laid out in the pavilion. هذة is the print’s spelling of هذه.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسْتُ فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَقْعَدِ أَنْتَظِرُ مَجِيءَ مَحْبُوبَةِ قَلْبِي إِلَى أَنْ مَضَى أَوَّلُ سَاعَةٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ وَثَانِي سَاعَةٍ وَثَالِثُ سَاعَةٍ فَلَمْ تَأْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalastu fī dhālika al-maqʿadi antaẓiru majīʾa maḥbūbati qalbī ilā an maḍā awwalu sāʿatin mina al-layli wa-thānī sāʿatin wa-thālithu sāʿatin fa-lam taʾti
sentences.l: So I sat in that sitting-place awaiting the coming of the beloved of my heart, until there passed the first hour of the night, and the second hour, and the third hour; and she did not come.
sentences.i: So I sat down in the alcove to wait for my heart’s beloved, until the first hour of the night had passed, and the second, and the third; and still she did not come.
sentences.n: al-maqʿad: “the sitting-place”, the raised seat or alcove of the pavilion.

sentences.t: وَاشْتَدَّ بِي أَلَمُ الْجُوعِ لِأَنَّ لِي مُدَّةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ مَا أَكَلْتُ طَعَامًا لِشِدَّةِ وَجْدِي
sentences.tr: wa-ishtadda bī alamu al-jūʿi li-anna lī muddatan mina al-zamāni mā akaltu ṭaʿāman li-shiddati wajdī
sentences.l: And the pain of hunger grew strong in me, because for me (there had been) a span of time (that) I had not eaten food, for the vehemence of my passion.
sentences.i: Hunger began to gnaw at me, for it was a long while since I had eaten anything, so violent was my passion.
sentences.n: li-anna lī muddatan … mā akaltu, “because I had a span of time in which I had not eaten”: the colloquial way of saying “for some time now I had not eaten”. The same turn comes again a few lines on.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانَ وَظَهَرَ لِي صِدْقُ بِنْتِ عَمِّي فِي فَهْمِ إِشَارَةِ مَعْشُوقَتِى اسْتَرَحْتُ وَوَجَدْتُ أَلَمَ الْجُوعِ وَقَدْ شَوَّقَتْنِي رَوَائِحُ الطَّعَامِ الَّذِي فِى السُّفْرَةِ لَمَّا وَصَلْتُ إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَاطْمَأَنَّتْ نَفْسِي بِالْوِصَالِ فَاشْتَهَتْ نَفْسِي الْأَكْلَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytu dhālika al-makāna wa-ẓahara lī ṣidqu binti ʿammī fī fahmi ishārati maʿshūqatī istaraḥtu wa-wajadtu alama al-jūʿi wa-qad shawwaqatnī rawāʾiḥu al-ṭaʿāmi alladhī fī al-sufrati lammā waṣaltu ilā dhālika al-makāni wa-iṭmaʾannat nafsī bi-al-wiṣāli fa-ishtahat nafsī al-akla
sentences.l: So when I saw that place, and there appeared to me the truthfulness of the daughter of my uncle in understanding the sign of my beloved, I was at ease, and I felt the pain of hunger; and the smells of the food that was on the cloth had made me long, when I reached that place, and my soul was set at rest by the union; so my soul craved eating.
sentences.i: Now that I had seen the place, and could see that my cousin had read my beloved’s signs truly, my mind was at ease and I felt my hunger. The smell of the food on the cloth had been tempting me ever since I arrived, and now that I was sure of our meeting, I longed to eat.
sentences.n: al-sufra: the cloth or low round tray on which a meal is spread. bi-al-wiṣāl, “by the union”: bi-, “by, through”, names what set his mind at rest, the promise of meeting her.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمْتُ إِلَى السُّفْرَةِ وَكَشَفْتُ الْغِطَاءَ فَوَجَدْتُ فِي وَسَطِهَا طَبَقًا مِنَ الصِّينِىِّ وَفِيهِ أَرْبَعُ دَجَاجَاتٍ مُحَمَّرَةٍ وَمُتَبَّلَةٍ بِالْبَهَارَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddamtu ilā al-sufrati wa-kashaftu al-ghiṭāʾa fa-wajadtu fī wasaṭihā ṭabaqan mina al-ṣīniyyi wa-fīhi arbaʿu dajājātin muḥammaratin wa-mutabbalatin bi-al-bahārāti
sentences.l: So I went forward to the cloth and uncovered the cover, and I found in its middle a platter of china, and in it four hens, browned and seasoned with spices.
sentences.i: I went up to the cloth and lifted the cover, and found in the middle a china platter with four roast chickens on it, browned and seasoned with spices.
sentences.n: al-ṣīnī, “the Chinese (ware)”: porcelain. muḥammara, “reddened”: roasted brown. bi-al-bahārāt: bi-, “with”, names the seasoning.

sentences.t: وَحَوْلَ ذَلِكَ الطَّبَقِ أَرْبَعُ زَبَادِى وَاحِدَةٌ حَلْوَى وَالْأُخْرَى حَبُّ الرُّمَّانِ وَالثَّالِثَةُ بَقْلَاوَةٌ وَالرَّابِعَةُ قَطَائِفُ وَتِلْكَ الزَّبَادِى مَابَيْنَ حَلْوَى وَحَامِضٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥawla dhālika al-ṭabaqi arbaʿu zabādī wāḥidatun ḥalwā wa-al-ukhrā ḥabbu al-rummāni wa-al-thālithatu baqlāwatun wa-al-rābiʿatu qaṭāʾifu wa-tilka al-zabādī mā bayna ḥalwā wa-ḥāmiḍin
sentences.l: And around that platter four bowls: one sweetmeat, and the other the seeds of the pomegranate, and the third baqlāwa, and the fourth qaṭāʾif; and those bowls (were) between sweet and sour.
sentences.i: Around the platter stood four bowls: one of sweetmeat, one of pomegranate seeds, one of baklava and one of qaṭāʾif, some sweet and some sour.
sentences.n: zabādī: bowls, plural of zubdiyya. ḥalwā: a sweetmeat or paste. qaṭāʾif: small pancakes, folded and filled and steeped in syrup. مابين is printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَأَكَلْتُ مِنَ الْقَطَائِفِ وَقِطْعَةَ لَحْمٍ وَعَمَدْتُ إِلَى الْبَقْلَاوَةِ وَأَكَلْتُ مِنْهَا مَا تَيَسَّرَ ثُمَّ قَصَدْتُ الْحَلْوَى وَأَكَلْتُ مِلْعَقَةً أَوِ اثْنَتَيْنِ أَوْ ثَلٰثًا أَوْ أَرْبَعًا وَأَكَلْتُ بَعْضَ دَجَاجَةٍ وَأَكَلْتُ لُقْمَةً
sentences.tr: fa-akaltu mina al-qaṭāʾifi wa-qiṭʿata laḥmin wa-ʿamadtu ilā al-baqlāwati wa-akaltu minhā mā tayassara thumma qaṣadtu al-ḥalwā wa-akaltu milʿaqatan awi ithnatayni aw thalāthan aw arbaʿan wa-akaltu baʿḍa dajājatin wa-akaltu luqmatan
sentences.l: So I ate of the qaṭāʾif, and a piece of meat, and I turned to the baqlāwa and ate of it what came easily; then I made for the sweetmeat and ate a spoonful, or two, or three, or four; and I ate some of a hen, and I ate a mouthful.
sentences.i: I ate some of the qaṭāʾif and a piece of meat; then I turned to the baklava and ate as much as I liked; then I went for the sweetmeat and ate a spoonful, or two, or three, or four; and I ate part of a chicken, and another mouthful.
sentences.n: mā tayassara, “what came easily”: as much as he pleased. thalāthan is printed ثلٰثا, the old spelling without the long alif, here with the small upright alif that marks it.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ امْتَلَأَتْ بَطْنِي وَارْتَخَتْ مَفَاصِلِي وَقَدْ كَسِلْتُ عَنِ السَّهَرِ فَوَضَعْتُ رَأْسِي عَلَى وِسَادَةٍ بَعْدَ أَنْ غَسَلْتُ يَدِى فَغَلَبَنِي النَّوْمُ وَلَمْ أَعْلَمْ بِمَا جَرَى لِي بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika imtalaʾat baṭnī wa-irtakhat mafāṣilī wa-qad kasiltu ʿani al-sahari fa-waḍaʿtu raʾsī ʿalā wisādatin baʿda an ghasaltu yadī fa-ghalabanī al-nawmu wa-lam aʿlam bi-mā jarā lī baʿda dhālika
sentences.l: And at that, my belly was filled and my joints went slack, and I had grown too sluggish for keeping awake; so I put my head on a cushion, after I had washed my hand, and sleep overcame me, and I did not know of what happened to me after that.
sentences.i: At that my belly was full, my limbs grew heavy, and I was too drowsy to stay awake. I washed my hands and laid my head on a cushion, and sleep overcame me; and I knew nothing of what happened to me after that.
sentences.n: imtalaʾat baṭnī, “my belly was filled (she)”: baṭn, belly, is masculine in Classical Arabic but treated as feminine here, as often in the spoken language. kasiltu ʿan, “I was too lazy for”: ʿan marks what laziness keeps one from. lam aʿlam bi-mā, “I did not know of what”: the verb takes bi- for what is known.

sentences.t: فَمَا اسْتَيْقَظْتُ حَتَّى أَحْرَقَنِي حَرُّ الشَّمْسِ لِأَنَّ لِي أَيَّامًا مَا ذُقْتُ مَنَامًا
sentences.tr: fa-mā istayqaẓtu ḥattā aḥraqanī ḥarru al-shamsi li-anna lī ayyāman mā dhuqtu manāman
sentences.l: And I did not wake until the heat of the sun burned me, because for me (it had been) days (that) I had not tasted sleep.
sentences.i: I did not wake until the heat of the sun was scorching me, for I had not slept for days.
sentences.n: mā dhuqtu manāman, “I had not tasted sleep”: the usual Arabic image for not sleeping at all.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَيْقَظْتُ وَجَدْتُ عَلَى بَطْنِي مِلْحًا وَفَحْمًا فَانْتَصَبْتُ قَائِمًا وَنَفَضْتُ ثِيَابِي وَقَدْ تَلَفَّتُّ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَلَمْ أَجِدْ أَحَدًا وَوَجَدْتُ نَفْسِي نَائِمًا عَلَى الرُّخَامِ مِنْ غَيْرِ فَرْشٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istayqaẓtu wajadtu ʿalā baṭnī milḥan wa-faḥman fa-intaṣabtu qāʾiman wa-nafaḍtu thiyābī wa-qad talaffattu yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-lam ajid aḥadan wa-wajadtu nafsī nāʾiman ʿalā al-rukhāmi min ghayri farshin
sentences.l: So when I woke, I found on my belly salt and charcoal; so I sprang up standing and shook out my clothes, and I had looked about right and left, and I did not find anyone; and I found myself sleeping on the marble without bedding.
sentences.i: When I woke, I found salt and charcoal laid on my belly. I sprang to my feet and shook out my clothes, and looked to right and left, but there was no one; and I found I had been sleeping on the bare marble, with nothing spread under me.
sentences.n: The print sets the word تلّفت, with the shadda on the lām; the verb is talaffattu, “I looked around”, with the doubling on the fā’, and it is pointed so here. The salt and the charcoal are a message, and his cousin will read it at the end of the night.

sentences.t: فَتَحَيَّرْتُ فِي عَقْلِي وَحَزِنْتُ حُزْنًا عَظِيمًا وَجَرَتْ دُمُوعِي عَلَى خَدِّي وَتَأَسَّفْتُ عَلَى نَفْسِي
sentences.tr: fa-taḥayyartu fī ʿaqlī wa-ḥazintu ḥuznan ʿaẓīman wa-jarat dumūʿī ʿalā khaddī wa-taʾassaftu ʿalā nafsī
sentences.l: So I was bewildered in my mind, and I grieved a great grief, and my tears ran on my cheek, and I felt sorrow over myself.
sentences.i: I was at my wits’ end. I grieved bitterly, the tears ran down my cheeks, and I was sorry for myself.

sentences.t: فَقُمْتُ وَقَصَدْتُ الْبَيْتَ فَلَمَّا وَصَلْتُ إِلَيْهِ وَجَدْتُ ابْنَةَ عَمِّي تَدُقُّ بِيَدِهَا عَلَى صَدْرِهَا وَتَبْكِي بِدَمْعٍ يُبَارِي السُّحُبَ الْمَاطِرَاتِ وَتُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qumtu wa-qaṣadtu al-bayta fa-lammā waṣaltu ilayhi wajadtu ibnata ʿammī taduqqu bi-yadihā ʿalā ṣadrihā wa-tabkī bi-damʿin yubārī al-suḥuba al-māṭirāti wa-tunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: So I rose and made for the house; and when I reached it, I found the daughter of my uncle beating with her hand upon her breast and weeping with tears that vie with the raining clouds, and reciting these verses:
sentences.i: So I got up and went home; and when I arrived, I found my cousin beating her breast and weeping tears to rival the rain clouds, and reciting these verses:
sentences.n: taduqqu bi-yadihā, “beating with her hand”: bi-, “with”, names the instrument. yubārī, “vies with, competes with”.

sentences.t:
هَبَّ رِيحٌ مِنَ الْحِمَى وَنَسِيمٌ * فَاَهَاجَ الْهَوَى بِنَشْرِ هُبُوبِهْ
يَا نَسِيمَ الصَّبَا هَلُمَّ اِلَيْنَا * كُلُّ صَبٍّ بِحَظِّهِ وَنَصِيبِهْ
لَوْ قَدَرْنَا مِنَ الْعَرَامِ اعْتَنَقْنَا * كَاعْتِنَاقِ الْمُحِبِّ صَدْرَ حَبِيبِهْ
حَرَّمَ اللّٰهُ بَعْدَ وَجْهِ بْنِ عَمِّي * كُلَّ عَيْشٍ مِنَ الزَّمَانِ وَطِيبِهْ
لَيْتَ شِعْرِي هَلْ قَلْبُهُ مِثْلُ قَلْبِي * ذَائِبٌ مِنْ حَرِّ الْهَوَى وَلَهِيبِهْ
sentences.tr:
habba rīḥun mina al-ḥimā wa-nasīmun * fa-ahāja al-hawā bi-nashri hubūbih
yā nasīma al-ṣabā halumma ilaynā * kullu ṣabbin bi-ḥaẓẓihi wa-naṣībih
law qadarnā mina al-ʿarāmi iʿtanaqnā * ka-iʿtināqi al-muḥibbi ṣadra ḥabībih
ḥarrama allāhu baʿda wajhi bni ʿammī * kulla ʿayshin mina al-zamāni wa-ṭībih
layta shiʿrī hal qalbuhu mithlu qalbī * dhāʾibun min ḥarri al-hawā wa-lahībih
sentences.l:
A wind blew from the guarded pasture, and a breeze, * and it stirred up love with the spreading-scent of its blowing.
O breeze of the east wind, come to us! * Every lover (comes) with his lot and his share.
If we were able, from passion, we would embrace, * like the embracing of the lover the breast of his beloved.
God has forbidden, after the face of the son of my uncle, * every life of time, and its sweetness.
Would that I knew: is his heart like my heart, * melting from the heat of love and its flame?
sentences.i:
A wind came blowing from the beloved’s land, a gentle breeze, * and the scent it carried stirred up love again.
O east wind, breeze of morning, come to us: * every lover has his portion and his share.
If we could, for very passion we would cling together * as a lover clings to his beloved’s breast.
Now that my cousin’s face is gone, God has denied me * all life can give, and every joy it holds.
If only I knew whether his heart is like my own, * melting away in the heat and flame of love!
sentences.n: al-ḥimā, “the guarded pasture”: in love poetry the protected ground where the beloved’s people camp. al-ṣabā is the east wind, the lovers’ messenger. The print has الْعَرَامِ, al-ʿarām, “fierceness”, with ʿayn where ghayn would be expected (one dot missing); the sense very likely wants al-gharām, “passion”, but ʿarām is a real word, so the print is kept and translated by the likelier sense. bni ʿammī: ibn, printed without its alif, which is never sounded after a vowel (wajhi bni). The final hā’ of each line is held with a sukūn for the rhyme (hubūbih, naṣībih).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْنِي قَامَتْ مُسْرِعَةً وَمَسَحَتْ دُمُوعَهَا وَأَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيَّ بِلِينِ كَلَامِهَا وَقَالَتْ لِي يَا بْنَ عَمِّي أَنْتَ فِي عِشْقِكَ قَدْ لَطَفَ اللَّهُ بِكَ حَيْثُ أَحَبَّكَ مَنْ تُحِبُّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾatnī qāmat musriʿatan wa-masaḥat dumūʿahā wa-aqbalat ʿalayya bi-līni kalāmihā wa-qālat lī yā bna ʿammī anta fī ʿishqika qad laṭafa allāhu bika ḥaythu aḥabbaka man tuḥibbu
sentences.l: So when she saw me, she rose hastening and wiped her tears, and came toward me with the softness of her speech, and said to me: O son of my uncle, you, in your love, God has been gracious to you, since the one you love has loved you;
sentences.i: When she saw me she got up quickly, wiped away her tears, and came to me with gentle words. “Cousin,” she said, “God has been kind to you in your love, for the one you love loves you;
sentences.n: laṭafa allāhu bika, “God was gracious to you”: the verb takes bi- for the one shown kindness. aqbalat ʿalayya bi-līni kalāmihā: “she came toward me with soft words”, bi- naming what she brought.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا فِي بُكَائِي وَحُزْنِي عَلَى فِرَاقِكَ مَنْ يَلُمْنِي وَيَعْذِرُنِي وَلَكِنْ لَا يُؤَاخِذُكَ اللَّهُ مِنْ جِهَتِي
sentences.tr: wa-anā fī bukāʾī wa-ḥuznī ʿalā firāqika man yalumnī wa-yaʿdhirunī wa-lākin lā yuʾākhidhuka allāhu min jihatī
sentences.l: and I, in my weeping and my grief over parting from you, who blames me and excuses me? But may God not take you to task on my account.
sentences.i: but as for me, weeping and grieving because you are lost to me, who is there to blame me, or to excuse me? Still, may God not hold you to account on my account.”
sentences.n: yalumnī, “blames me”: the print’s form, a shortened yalūmunī, as the spoken language often has it. The sense of the question is that no one cares how she weeps. lā yuʾākhidhuka allāhu: a wish, “may God not punish you”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا تَبَسَّمَتْ فِي وَجْهِي تَبَسُّمَ الْغَيْظِ وَلَاطَفَتْنِي وَقَلَعَتْنِي أَثْوَابِي وَنَشَرَتْهَا وَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ مَا هَذِهِ رَوَائِحُ مَنْ حَظِيَ بِمَحْبُوبِهِ فَأَخْبِرْنِي بِمَا جَرَى لَكَ يَا بْنَ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: thumma innahā tabassamat fī wajhī tabassuma al-ghayẓi wa-lāṭafatnī wa-qalaʿatnī athwābī wa-nasharathā wa-qālat wa-allāhi mā hādhihi rawāʾiḥu man ḥaẓiya bi-maḥbūbihi fa-akhbirnī bi-mā jarā laka yā bna ʿammī
sentences.l: Then she smiled in my face the smile of vexation, and was gentle with me, and stripped me of my garments and spread them out, and said: By God, these are not the smells of one who has won favour with his beloved; so tell me of what happened to you, O son of my uncle.
sentences.i: Then she gave me a smile of vexation, coaxed me, took off my clothes and spread them out, and said, “By God, this is not the scent of a man who has won his beloved. Tell me what happened to you, cousin.”
sentences.n: qalaʿatnī athwābī, “she stripped me my clothes”: the verb takes two objects, the person and the clothes, as verbs of stripping often do (salabahu thawbahu, “he stripped him of his garment”). She spreads them out to smell them. ḥaẓiya bi-, “to win, enjoy the favour of”: bi- marks the one enjoyed. akhbirnī bi-mā, “tell me of what”: bi- marks the news.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِجَمِيعِ مَا جَرَى لِي فَتَبَسَّمَتْ تَبَسُّمَ الْغَيْظِ ثَانِيًا وَقَالَتْ إِنَّ قَلْبِي مَلْآنُ مُوجَعٌ فَلَا عَاشَ مَنْ يُوجِعُ قَلْبَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbartuhā bi-jamīʿi mā jarā lī fa-tabassamat tabassuma al-ghayẓi thāniyan wa-qālat inna qalbī malʾānu mūjaʿun fa-lā ʿāsha man yūjiʿu qalbaka
sentences.l: So I told her of all that had happened to me; and she smiled the smile of vexation a second time and said: My heart is full, pained; so may he not live who pains your heart!
sentences.i: So I told her everything that had happened, and again she smiled her vexed smile and said, “My heart is full and aching; may whoever pains your heart not live!
sentences.n: fa-lā ʿāsha, “may he not live”: the perfect after lā expresses a wish, here a curse. ملآن is printed with the long-alif sign.

sentences.t: وَهَذِهِ الْمَرْأَةُ تَتَعَزَّزُ عَلَيْكَ تَعَزُّزًا قَوِيًّا وَاللَّهِ يَا بْنَ عَمِّي إِنِّي خَائِفَةٌ عَلَيْكَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi al-marʾatu tataʿazzazu ʿalayka taʿazzuzan qawiyyan wa-allāhi yā bna ʿammī innī khāʾifatun ʿalayka minhā
sentences.l: And this woman holds herself dear against you, a strong holding-dear; by God, O son of my uncle, I am fearful for you from her.
sentences.i: This woman holds herself very high with you. By God, cousin, I fear what she will do to you.
sentences.n: tataʿazzazu ʿalayka, “she makes herself precious toward you”: she plays proud, keeps him at a distance. khāʾifatun ʿalayka minhā: ʿalā marks the one feared for, min the one feared.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ يَا بْنَ عَمِّي أَنَّ تَفْسِيرَ الْمِلْحِ هُوَ أَنَّكَ مُسْتَغْرِقٌ فِي النَّوْمِ فَكَأَنَّكَ بَشِعُ الطَّعْمِ بِحَيْثُ تَعَافُكَ النُّفُوسُ فَيَنْبَغِي لَكَ أَنْ تَتَمَلَّحَ حَتَّى لَا تَمُجَّكَ الطِّبَاعُ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam yā bna ʿammī anna tafsīra al-milḥi huwa annaka mustaghriqun fī al-nawmi fa-ka-annaka bashiʿu al-ṭaʿmi bi-ḥaythu taʿāfuka al-nufūsu fa-yanbaghī laka an tatamallaḥa ḥattā lā tamujjaka al-ṭibāʿu
sentences.l: And know, O son of my uncle, that the meaning of the salt is that you are sunk in sleep, so it is as if you are foul of taste, such that souls loathe you; so it behoves you to salt yourself, so that natures do not spit you out.
sentences.i: Know, cousin, that the salt means this: you are sunk in sleep, as if you tasted foul, so that people find you repellent. You should season yourself, so that no one spits you out.
sentences.n: tatamallaḥa, “to salt yourself”: the verb also means to become witty, charming, agreeable (milḥ, salt, is also wit and grace), and the sign plays on both. bashiʿ al-ṭaʿm, “foul of taste”: the print marks the bā’ with a fatḥa.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّكَ تَدَّعِي أَنَّكَ مِنَ الْعُشَّاقِ الْكِرَامِ وَالنَّوْمُ عَلَى الْعُشَّاقِ حَرَامٌ فَدَعْوَاكَ الْمَحَبَّةَ كَاذِبَةٌ
sentences.tr: li-annaka taddaʿī annaka mina al-ʿushshāqi al-kirāmi wa-al-nawmu ʿalā al-ʿushshāqi ḥarāmun fa-daʿwāka al-maḥabbata kādhibatun
sentences.l: Because you claim that you are of the noble lovers, and sleep is forbidden to lovers; so your claim to love is lying.
sentences.i: For you claim to be one of the noble lovers, and to lovers sleep is forbidden; so your claim to love is false.
sentences.n: al-nawmu ʿalā al-ʿushshāqi ḥarāmun, “sleep is forbidden to lovers”: a commonplace of love poetry, put as a rhyme (kirām / ḥarām). daʿwāka al-maḥabbata, “your claiming love”: the verbal noun takes love as its object.

sentences.t: وَكَذَلِكَ هِيَ مَحَبَّتُهَا لَكَ كَاذِبَةٌ لِأَنَّهَا لَمَّا رَأَتْكَ نَائِمًا لَمْ تُنَبِّهْكَ وَلَوْ كَانَتْ مَحَبَّتُهَا لَكَ صَادِقَةً لَنَبَّهَتْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-kadhālika hiya maḥabbatuhā laka kādhibatun li-annahā lammā raʾatka nāʾiman lam tunabbihka wa-law kānat maḥabbatuhā laka ṣādiqatan la-nabbahatka
sentences.l: And likewise it, her love for you, is lying, because when she saw you sleeping she did not wake you; and if her love for you were true, she would have woken you.
sentences.i: And her love for you is just as false: when she saw you asleep she did not wake you, and if she truly loved you, she would have.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْفَحْمُ فَإِنَّ تَفْسِيرَ إِشَارَتِهِ سَوَّدَ اللَّهُ وَجْهَكَ حَيْثُ ادَّعَيْتَ الْمَحَبَّةَ كِذْبًا وَإِنَّمَا أَنْتَ صَغِيرٌ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَكَ هِمَّةٌ إِلَّا الْأَكْلُ وَالشُّرْبُ وَالنَّوْمُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-faḥmu fa-inna tafsīra ishāratihi sawwada allāhu wajhaka ḥaythu iddaʿayta al-maḥabbata kidhban wa-innamā anta ṣaghīrun wa-lam yakun laka himmatun illā al-aklu wa-al-shurbu wa-al-nawmu
sentences.l: And as for the charcoal, the meaning of its sign is: May God blacken your face, since you have claimed love falsely; and you are only small, and there was not for you any concern except eating and drinking and sleeping.
sentences.i: As for the charcoal, its meaning is: God blacken your face, for claiming a love you do not feel. You are only a child, with no thought in your head but eating, drinking and sleeping.
sentences.n: sawwada allāhu wajhaka, “God blacken your face”: a curse meaning “God disgrace you”; the charcoal is the blackening.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا تَفْسِيرُ إِشَارَتِهَا فَاللَّهُ تَعَالَى يُخَلِّصُكَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā tafsīru ishāratihā fa-allāhu taʿālā yukhalliṣuka minhā
sentences.l: And this is the meaning of her sign; so God, exalted is He, may He deliver you from her!
sentences.i: That is what her signs mean. May God Almighty set you free of her!”

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ كَلَامَهَا ضَرَبْتُ بِيَدِي عَلَى صَدْرِي وَقُلْتُ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ هَذَا هُوَ الصَّحِيحُ لِأَنِّي نِمْتُ وَالْعُشَّاقُ لَا يَنَامُونَ فَأَنَا الظَّالِمُ لِنَفْسِي وَمَا كَانَ أَضَرَّ عَلَيَّ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ وَالنَّوْمِ فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ الْأَمْرُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu kalāmahā ḍarabtu bi-yadī ʿalā ṣadrī wa-qultu wa-allāhi inna hādhā huwa al-ṣaḥīḥu li-annī nimtu wa-al-ʿushshāqu lā yanāmūna fa-anā al-ẓālimu li-nafsī wa-mā kāna aḍarra ʿalayya mina al-akli wa-al-nawmi fa-kayfa yakūnu al-amru
sentences.l: So when I heard her speech, I struck with my hand upon my breast and said: By God, this is the right (of it), because I slept, and lovers do not sleep; so I am the wronger of myself; and nothing was more harmful to me than eating and sleeping. So how will the matter be?
sentences.i: When I heard what she said, I beat my breast and cried, “By God, that is the truth of it! I slept, and lovers do not sleep. I have wronged no one but myself. Nothing could have done me more harm than eating and sleeping. What am I to do now?”
sentences.n: wa-mā kāna aḍarra ʿalayya mina …, “nothing was more harmful to me than …”: mā negates, and aḍarra … min is the comparative, “more harmful than”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي زِدْتُ فِى الْبُكَاءِ وَقُلْتُ لِابْنَةِ عَمِّى دُلِّينِي عَلَى شَيْءٍ أَفْعَلُهُ وَارْحَمِينِي يَرْحَمُكِ اللَّهُ وَإِلَّا أَمُوتُ
sentences.tr: thumma innī zidtu fī al-bukāʾi wa-qultu li-ibnati ʿammī dullīnī ʿalā shayʾin afʿaluhu wa-irḥamīnī yarḥamuki allāhu wa-illā amūtu
sentences.l: Then I increased in weeping and said to the daughter of my uncle: Guide me to a thing I may do, and have mercy on me, may God have mercy on you; or else I die.
sentences.i: Then I wept all the more, and said to my cousin, “Tell me something I can do. Have pity on me, and God have pity on you, or I shall die.”
sentences.n: dullīnī ʿalā, “guide me to”: the verb takes ʿalā for what one is shown. zidtu fī al-bukāʾ: “I increased in weeping”, fī marking what grows.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ بِنْتُ عَمِّي تُحِبُّنِي مَحَبَّةً عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: wa-kānat bintu ʿammī tuḥibbunī maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: And the daughter of my uncle loved me with a great love.
sentences.i: And my cousin loved me dearly.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
